title: TSMC To Commence A14 Process Node Mass Production in the First Half of 2028, Eyeing a 7.5x Capacity Versus Intel’s 14A and Scaling SRAM After Almost A
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

TSMC is reportedly preparing to begin mass production of its A14 process in the first half of 2028, setting up another contest with Intel in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. The timing would refine TSMC’s official guidance, which currently places A14 volume production in 2028 without specifying a half.

According to Wccftech, citing DigiTimes, TSMC could have 7.5 times Intel’s 14A manufacturing capacity during 2028. That comparison remains a reported projection rather than a confirmed production outcome. If achieved, the gap would highlight TSMC’s ability to support large customer launches alongside the technical advances promised by its next generation.

A14 uses TSMC’s second generation of nanosheet transistors. The company says the technology will deliver 10–15% higher speed at the same power consumption, or reduce power consumption by 25–30% at the same speed, compared with N2. TSMC also targets more than 20% higher logic density, supported by its NanoFlex Pro architecture.

Another potentially significant development concerns SRAM, the fast memory used for processor caches. Electronic Times reports that A14 could shrink high-density SRAM bit cells below 0.017 square micrometers, compared with approximately 0.021 square micrometers since N5. That would represent renewed scaling after roughly eight years when A14 reaches planned volume production.

Smaller SRAM cells could help designers fit larger caches into a given chip area or reduce the space required for existing cache capacities. These gains matter for CPUs, GPUs and AI accelerators, where moving data efficiently can be as important as increasing computing throughput. Actual benefits will depend on implementation.

For now, the distinction between official targets and industry reporting remains essential. TSMC has confirmed the broader 2028 schedule and performance objectives, while the first-half launch, capacity multiple and SRAM dimensions require further confirmation. Successful execution would strengthen its competitive position, although manufacturing yields, costs and customer adoption will determine results.
